preamble: Classical Arabic ḍād ض, reconstructed as a pharyngealized voiced lateral fricative [ɮˤ] (Versteegh 1999, 2000, cited by Wikipedia; Wiktionary), is pronounced as the pharyngealized stop [dˤ] in Modern Standard Arabic and in most of Egypt, Sudan, Syria, Lebanon and Palestine (Wikipedia, Ḍād). The lateral is lost and the fricative becomes a stop. The correspondence is telescoped. According to Wiktionary, ḍād first merged in speech with ẓāʾ [ðˤ], a merger reflected in the colloquial dialects; in dialects that stopped the dental fricatives both then became [dˤ]; and Qur'an readers, once [ɮˤ] was no longer produced, reassigned the stop [dˤ] to ض to keep it apart from ظ. The Standard Arabic [dˤ] is thus a reading pronunciation, and the Egyptian and Levantine [dˤ] goes through [ðˤ]. Not every variety merged: dialects of the Saudi Tihāmah keep lateral reflexes, and some distinguish the reflexes of ḍ and ẓ (Watson & Al-Azraqi 2011: 427–428). The starting value is itself a reconstruction from Sibawayh's description; André Roman proposed [ʑˤ] instead (Wikipedia, Ḍād). Some Egyptian accents have a plain [d] (Wikipedia, Ḍād).
